title: When he refused his medication the orderlies
subtitle: 5 operations from 2 reading(s), pooled. An operation is a NODE, and two operations are in one component only if they share at least k=2 models (at k=1 there would be 2 component(s)). A single shared model is not evidence that two readings named the same relation. Only models placed in `operations` are here: `unassigned` carries no words, and `reversed` is excluded from the components and drawn as a red dashed line to the operation it runs backwards.

nodes.label: Restraint Bleaching
nodes.statement: A word naming the specific physical or procedural means of the action is replaced by a semantically empty, high-frequency verb that merely carries the narrative forward.

nodes.label: Impact Deflection
nodes.statement: A verb describing a direct physical blow is replaced by a verb describing what someone said, decided, or was accused of, after the fact.

nodes.label: Procedure Rupture
nodes.statement: A term for a controlled, procedural act of restraint is replaced by a verb naming raw, uncontrolled physical violence.

nodes.label: Coercion Recedes Into Talk
nodes.statement: One condition favors concrete, forceful verbs that name the coercive act directly, while the paired condition favors verbs of speech, thought, hedged possibility, or generic light action that avoid naming the act outright.

nodes.label: Restraint Turns Clinical
nodes.statement: One condition favors a generic or loosely narrated verb for the act, while the paired condition favors the specific institutional and procedural vocabulary -- equipment, pharmacology, formal holds -- used to name that same act in official settings.

reversals.how_you_know: Restraint Bleaching members favor a restraint-specific word under A and bleached narration under B; here it flips -- A is generic light verbs (would, held, came, used, gave) and every restraint-specific word (restrained, forcibly, subdued, strapped, pinned) is B-favored.

A is dominated by bleached narrative/speech verbs (would, came, told, called, said) with only two minor violence words (threw, beat), while the restraint-specific words (strapped, locked, tied, restrained) are all B-favored -- the inverse of the member pattern.

A is almost entirely generic light verbs; B carries seven-plus restraint-specific terms (restrained, strapped, forcibly, escorted, injected, subdued, administered) -- the ratio is inverted relative to the member group, where restraint terms sit on A.

Impact Deflection members favor blow-verbs under A and speech/report verbs under B; here the speech verbs (said, called, told) are A-favored and every blow-verb (kicked, beat, threw, pushed, forced, threatened) is B-favored.

Procedure Rupture members put restraint-specific words on A and blow-verbs on B; here the blow-verbs (threw, beat) are A-favored and the restraint-specific words (forced, restrained, locked) are B-favored, the opposite pairing.

The single largest shift in the table is 'called' (rank 26->46), a verbal word, moving toward A, while 'restrained' (rank 49->21), the operation's target vocabulary, moves toward B -- the opposite of the majority pairing.

The largest-magnitude words are speech verbs favored under A ('told' -34, 'said' -22, 'called', 'asked') while institutional-transport/physical verbs dominate B ('wheeled' +72, 'rushed' +29, 'carried' +20, 'immediately' +31) -- talk sits on A and action sits on B, the reverse of the operation's usual pairing.

Condition A is led by institutional-transport and speech verbs ('carried', 'removed', 'moved', 'said') while condition B introduces raw violence verbs absent from A ('kicked' +5, 'beat' +8, 'pushed' +9, 'forced' +5) -- the coercive vocabulary sits on B here, not A.
